newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan shareholders meet amid scandal uproar.
newsitem.headline: Japan shareholders meet amid scandal uproar.

text.p: Japanese firms braced for tense shareholders' meetings on Friday amid public outrage over an epidemic of corporate scandals involving payoffs to racketeers and other management misdeeds.

Among the blue-chip companies that could face tough questions from the floor are giant brokerage Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, both embroiled in a high-profile racketeer scandal that has led to more than a dozen arrests.

Japanese firms have long bunched their annual shareholders' meetings on a single day -- a tradition which helps them to dodge questions about scandals and mismanagement both from legitimate shareholders and from professional corporate extortionists called "sokaiya" who target such events.

Sokaiya try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices or stir up other trouble at shareholders' meetings. Some firms have also employed sokaiya to muzzle regular shareholders.
Police were out in force on Friday to help fend off the sokaiya threat, with more than 2,300 firms holding meetings.
But critics say what is really needed is reform of the secretive management mindset which encourages companies to shun disclosure.

"Most executives are more than able to answer such (embarrassing) questions and if the meetings were conducted that way the whole problem of sokaiya would disappear," said Charles Stevens, partner in international law firm Freshfields. "The culture is obsessed with quick and quiet shareholders' meetings and that sets the stage for a lot of other bad conduct including sokaiya payoffs and cover-ups of scandals," he said.
Legitimate shareholders could find plenty of questions to ask on Friday, although investors schooled in the virtues of silence often decline to speak out.
A shareholders' activist group has prepared a long list of queries for executives at Osaka-based trading house Sumitomo Corp over last year's huge losses by a rogue copper trader.
"We want to make Sumitomo into a model case," said Tokuo Sakaguchi of Shareholders Ombudsman, a group of lawyers, accountants and shareholders monitoring corporate activities.

Meetings at the other "Big Four" brokerages -- Daiwa Securities Co Ltd, Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd -- are also likely to come under close scrutiny given concern that the Nomura scandal could spread to other firms.
Executives at foodstuff maker Ajinomoto Co Inc could come under fire over its own sokaiya scandal, which forced the president to resign after two employees were arrested in April.

Shareholders of toymaker Bandai Co Ltd, meanwhile, may want to ask pointed questions about a corporate struggle which ended in the abrupt cancellation of its planned merger with videogame maker Sega Enterprises Ltd in May.
And All Nippon Airways Co Ltd, buffetted by a series of internal wrangles which resulted in a huge management reshuffle in May, could also see turbulence at Friday's gathering.
Stung by the criticism of excessive secrecy, several firms are opening their meetings to the media and the public or have held them on other days to ensure accessibility.
But corporate Japan is also seeking legal reforms that would reduce the items needing shareholders' approval, a move big business says is one key to reducing the sokaiya threat.

"Japan's Commercial Code stipulates that there must be 'sufficient debate' on items up for approval at shareholders' meetings and so the discussion can go on forever. That's why sokaiya can be active," said an official at business lobby Keidanren, which wants to change the law so that only the appointment of directors and auditors needs such approval.
"In America, they can cut off a questioner after just three minutes," he added.

Businessmen also fault police for not providing real protection from sokaiya, who are often linked to crime syndicates. "They can't really protect the executives and people get killed," the Keidanren official said.
Police, for example, blamed a sokaiya for the 1994 murder of a Fuji Photo official, and other killings and attacks have been reported over the years.
Critics, however, are not convinced that decreasing shareholders' clout is the way to go. "Keidanren's initiative sounds to me to be extremely counterproductive," Stevens said.
